title: The AI operating model playbook for regulated firms
linkedinPost:
94% of financial services firms are deploying AI.

Only firms with dedicated AI ownership consistently convert it to measurable outcomes — a 19-point gap vs those without. (AI Operations Report 2026: Financial Services, Coastal Cloud.)

The gap is not a model problem. It is an operating model problem.

What I would actually do to close it:

• Baseline revenue per employee by function — not company-wide. Compliance, ops, and credit have different AI leverage profiles. The function-level baseline is the only number that gives you a testable target.
• Run an AI inventory before classifying anything. You cannot govern what you have not enumerated. EU AI Act Annex III makes this a regulatory requirement and a business design step.
• Build one workflow to production standard. A credit memo agent or KYC pre-screening pipeline, with typed contracts, a human review gate, and an Article 12 audit log from day one. One production example is worth more than 10 pilots.
• Wire DORA and EU AI Act Article 12 logging into the same infrastructure. Both need the same data structure. Build once, serve both obligations.
• Set a 12-month RPE target by function. Without a target, operating model redesign has no success criterion.

Revenue per employee rises when the operating model is designed around it — not reported against it.

Full piece + the 4-Layer AI Operating Model I use to structure this — link in comments.

mainEntity.name: What is an AI operating model in banking?

acceptedAnswer.text: An AI operating model defines how a bank deploys AI into production workflows, who owns AI decisions, how performance is tracked, and how governance is enforced. It is the design layer between AI strategy and AI execution. Firms with a structured AI ownership model report measurable business value 19 percentage points more often than those without one. (AI Operations Report 2026: Financial Services, Coastal Cloud.)

mainEntity.name: How do I implement AI in a regulated financial services firm without compliance risk?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with an AI inventory before deploying at scale. Classify each system against EU AI Act Annex III criteria. Build audit logging into every workflow from day one — as a design requirement, not a retrofit. Place documented human review gates at every decision point that feeds a regulated outcome. Measure cost-to-serve and revenue per employee by function to confirm the operating model impact.

mainEntity.name: What does the EU AI Act require from banks' AI systems in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: High-risk systems — credit scoring, KYC/AML, insurance, employment screening — must meet requirements for risk management documentation, human oversight, data governance, and ongoing monitoring from August 2, 2026 (EU AI Act 2024/1689, Art. 113). Two earlier obligations are already active: AI literacy documentation (Article 4, February 2025) and prohibited practices review (Article 5, February 2025). A firm that has not run documented AI literacy training is already non-compliant.

mainEntity.name: What is the best way to measure AI ROI in financial services?

acceptedAnswer.text: Revenue per employee by function is the primary operating model metric. Supplement with cost-to-serve per transaction, time-to-decision on credit assessment or onboarding, and false-positive rate reduction in AML screening. Adoption metrics — users trained, models deployed — are lagging indicators of activity, not outcomes. The metric that holds up in a board conversation is: what did this do to revenue per employee in this function over the last 12 months?
